clinicalPearls: The classic acute overdose triad is refractory seizures, severe high anion-gap metabolic (lactic) acidosis and coma
Seizures typically begin within an hour or two of a significant ingestion and are often resistant to standard anticonvulsants
Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) is the specific antidote and usually terminates the seizures when benzodiazepines alone fail
Suspect isoniazid in any patient being treated for tuberculosis who presents with unexplained seizures and profound acidosis
The lactic acidosis is driven largely by seizure activity but also by impaired lactate metabolism, and it may persist until seizures are controlled
Benzodiazepines act synergistically with pyridoxine and are the first-line anticonvulsant while pyridoxine is prepared
Chronic therapeutic use can cause a separate spectrum of toxicity including peripheral neuropathy (prevented by pyridoxine) and hepatotoxicity
If the ingested amount is unknown and seizures are present, empirical pyridoxine is given, with dosing guided by the poisons centre
reference.pathophysiology: Isoniazid inhibits the enzyme that regenerates the active form of pyridoxine (pyridoxal-5-phosphate) and also complexes directly with pyridoxine, depleting this essential cofactor. Because pyridoxal-5-phosphate is required for synthesis of the inhibitory neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid, its depletion reduces central inhibition and precipitates seizures. Sustained seizure activity, together with impaired conversion of lactate to pyruvate, produces a severe high anion-gap lactic acidosis. Restoring pyridoxine replenishes the cofactor and allows gamma-aminobutyric acid synthesis to resume, which is why it controls the otherwise refractory seizures.
additionalDifferentials: Other toxin-induced seizures with acidosis (e.g. theophylline, sympathomimetics)
Primary central nervous system infection or structural lesion
Metabolic causes of seizure such as hypoglycaemia or hyponatraemia
Toxic alcohol poisoning causing high anion-gap acidosis
additionalInvestigations: Capillary and laboratory glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia as a seizure cause
Arterial blood gas with lactate and anion-gap assessment
Serum electrolytes, renal and liver function
Creatine kinase for rhabdomyolysis after prolonged seizures
Paracetamol and salicylate levels in intentional overdose
Continuous monitoring and neuroimaging if the cause is unclear
redFlags: Recurrent or refractory seizures unresponsive to benzodiazepines
Severe or persistent high anion-gap lactic acidosis
Coma or need for airway protection
Rhabdomyolysis or acute kidney injury after prolonged seizure activity
Ingestion by a patient on antituberculous therapy with unknown quantity
reference.prognosis: With early pyridoxine and benzodiazepines to control seizures and correct the acidosis, most patients recover fully; delayed treatment with prolonged seizures and profound acidosis is associated with significant morbidity and mortality.
pitfalls: Persisting with standard anticonvulsants without giving pyridoxine
Failing to consider isoniazid in tuberculosis patients presenting with seizures
Attributing the acidosis solely to seizures and undertreating the underlying cause
Not securing sufficient pyridoxine, which may be needed in substantial quantity
Overlooking chronic hepatotoxicity and neuropathy in long-term therapeutic users
management: Intravenous pyridoxine (vitamin B6) as the specific antidote to terminate isoniazid-induced seizures, given empirically when the ingested amount is unknown
Benzodiazepines as the first-line anticonvulsant, acting synergistically with pyridoxine to control seizures
Airway protection, oxygenation and supportive care for coma and respiratory depression
Correction of the high anion-gap lactic acidosis, which typically resolves once seizures are controlled
Activated charcoal for early presentation after a significant ingestion once the airway is secured
Haemodialysis for refractory acidosis or massive ingestion not responding to antidotal therapy
Monitor for rhabdomyolysis after prolonged seizures, screen for co-ingestants and involve clinical toxicology and critical care
